findings.title: The module the brief writes off as a rewrite is ~25% portable VT decoder, already tested — and it is exactly what Task 3 needs
findings.body:
You asked whether the reference-count proxy fails. It does fail, and on this axis it fails in the plan's favour. I re-ran the count per file and reproduced 64/2/2 with 19 zeros exactly. But I then listed the line numbers of every unix hit inside terminal.rs, and they stop at 1250 and do not resume until 1956 — and 1910 is where the first `#[cfg(test)]` module begins. Established: lines 1251–1909 of terminal.rs, roughly 660 lines of production code, contain zero references to rustix, std::os::unix, termios, libc or /dev/tty. What lives there is the entire VT input decoder: `parse_event_kitty` (1337), `parse_plain_bytes` (1383), `byte_key_event` (1430), `parse_csi` (1452), `parse_kitty_key` (1630), `parse_sgr_mouse` (1771), `parse_kitty_keyboard` (1811), `parse_osc_color` (1860), plus the bracketed-paste and clipboard-packet parsers. These are pure byte-slice functions.

What follows from that: Task 3's hardest-sounding checkbox — 'decode SGR mouse reports (?1006) and kitty keyboard sequences' — is not work to be done, it is work to be linked against. The plan already half-knows this ('feed the bytes to the existing VT input decoder rather than writing a second decoder') but the brief's 64-hit accounting hides how much of terminal.rs that decoder is, so the cost line for 'replace one module' is materially overstated.

The test position is stronger still. The test module at 1910 holds 29 tests; enumerating their names, at least 25 are pure byte-sequence parser tests — `parses_sgr_mouse_events`, `sgr_mouse_decodes_modifier_bits`, `parses_modifiers_on_legacy_and_kitty_keys`, `parses_kitty_repeat_and_release_events`, `parses_kitty_associated_text_and_function_keys`, `ctrl_bytes_and_alt_prefixes_decode_as_modified_chars`, `utf8_input_decodes_whole_chars`, `bracketed_paste_arrives_as_one_normalized_event`, and `parse_event_consumes_one_event_and_reports_incomplete_tails`. That last one is literally the 'a sequence split across two reads' case Task 3 lists as a test to be written. Only `shm_roundtrip` (1951) and `a_frame_file_is_rewritten_in_place_and_removed_on_drop` in that module are unix-bound; the 4 tests in `tty_tests` (2480+) are openpty-based and separate.

This bears on your stated fear about autonomous execution more than on cost. The riskiest thing about Windows console input is not calling SetConsoleMode — it is decoding kitty keyboard and SGR mouse correctly, where a subtle error produces plausible-looking wrong input that no milestone screenshot catches. That component arrives pre-written and pre-verified against ~25 recorded-byte tests that run unchanged on Windows.

What would overturn it: if the decoder functions turn out to take fd-typed or Termios-typed arguments from their callers rather than plain byte slices, the reuse would need more shimming than I am claiming. I read the signatures of `parse_csi`, `parse_sgr_mouse` and `parse_event_kitty` and they take `&[u8]`, but I did not trace every caller in the 1251–1909 range.
findings.fix: Rewrite Task 3's decode bullet to say the decoder is reused, and move the four listed decoder-test bullets into Task 2's seam extraction as 'keep these tests running', so a ralphex run cannot quietly reimplement a parser that already exists.

findings.title: Task 8 needs no agwinterm change at all, and its workload sits inside the already-shipping envelope of image.frame
findings.body:
This is your question 3 and question 4, and they answer together. I read agwinterm's `HandleImageFrame` at `src/Agwinterm.Pty/ControlServer.cs:426` in full. Established, not inferred: it takes `args.images[]`; each entry supplies `path`, `row`, `col`, `cols`, `rows` and optional source crop; it computes a `ContentSignature` from mtime/length/path and skips the file read when the id's signature is unchanged; phase 1 reads the bytes off the render lock and phase 2 takes `MutateLocked` only for `ClearPlacements` + `SetImageData(id, KittyFormat.Png, 0, 0, data)` + `PlaceImage(...)`. Every capability Task 5 asks for — cell-span scaling via cols/rows, id reuse against the content cache — is present in shipped code, and the dispatch entry is at line 249 exactly as the brief cites.

What follows: Tasks 1–8 have zero dependency on the agwinterm plan. The entire cross-repo contract risk is confined to Task 10, which is an optimization, and the plan already makes Task 10 self-guarding — its precondition bullet says stop rather than guess the layout, and it requires automatic fallback. I checked that the fallback is implementable against a real string rather than an assumed one: `ControlServer.cs:523` is `Err(string error) => {"ok":false,"error":<json>}` and the dispatch default at line 250 is `Err($"unknown command '{cmd}'")`. So Task 10's test 'the fallback triggers on an {"ok":false,"error":"unknown command..."} reply' is written against text that exists today.

And the milestone's workload is inside the proven envelope. agwinterm's own gap analysis (`docs/agterm-gap-analysis.md:41`) records that the file-based control-pipe path is the shipping Kitty-graphics route, used by docxy; agwinterm's design spec (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-06-30-agwinterm-design.md:204`) records that docxy emits static images. Task 8's deliverable is 'a static page legibly on screen' — a static image, which is precisely the workload image.frame is already in production for. The performance question that motivates shm is the *animated* case, and Task 8 is correctly placed to produce the measurement that justifies it rather than assuming it.

What would overturn it: if a full-pane 1920x1080 PNG encode plus file write plus agwinterm's PNG decode is slow enough that even a single static page takes seconds to appear, Task 8 would stall on a performance problem it was not scoped to solve. I could not measure this — measuring means running a build, which is outside this review — and the number does not exist yet on either side; the agwinterm plan's Task 6 is where it gets produced.

findings.title: Both portability risks you named by hand — arboard and fontdue — resolve clean, and the font path has no system dependency at all
findings.body:
You flagged arboard and fontdue specifically as places the zero-hit column might be lying. I checked both against the actual crate manifests in the local cargo registry rather than reasoning from reputation.

arboard 3.6.1: its Cargo.toml declares `[target."cfg(windows)".dependencies.clipboard-win]` and `windows-sys`, i.e. a first-class Windows backend. The feature the workspace enables, `wayland-data-control`, maps to the optional `wl-clipboard-rs`, which is declared under `[target.'cfg(all(unix, not(any(target_os="macos", target_os="android", target_os="emscripten"))))'.dependencies]` — a target-gated optional dependency is not built for a non-matching target, so enabling that feature on Windows pulls nothing in. Established separately: pixel-core has exactly one arboard call site, `clipboard_image.rs:56`, and it is `arboard::Clipboard::new().ok()?` — so even a runtime failure to open the clipboard degrades to `None` rather than a panic or a build break.

fontdue 0.9.3: no `[target.…]` sections at all; its only non-optional dependency is `ttf-parser` with default features off. Pure Rust rasterizer, nothing to port.

The font concern resolves harder than 'portable'. I grepped pixel-core for font acquisition and every hit is `include_bytes!("../../../assets/fonts/JetBrainsMono-Regular.ttf")` — menu.rs:356, paint.rs:775, text_input.rs:917, wrap.rs:139, tree/tests.rs:8. There is no system font enumeration, no fontconfig, no CoreText, no DirectWrite call anywhere in the crate; the typeface is compiled in. That also means the test fixtures are self-contained, which is what makes the regression net portable.

What would overturn it: a build is the only real proof, and I did not run one. Specifically, cargo's handling of a feature that names a target-gated optional dependency is what my arboard conclusion rests on; if the workspace's feature unification pulled `wl-clipboard-rs` in on a Windows target anyway, that crate would fail to build. The 41-error baseline you already measured is the evidence against that worry — those errors are in pixel-core's own source, not in a dependency.

findings.title: Task 2's real deliverable buys a live 200-test tripwire for exactly the failure mode you are afraid of
findings.body:
Your standard is that a wrong assumption becomes a long autonomous run that builds the wrong thing and looks like it succeeded. The strongest structural argument for this plan's ordering is that Task 2 is placed to defeat that specific failure mode, and the plan says so almost in passing — its bullet 'verify cargo check --workspace is clean on Windows — this is the task's real deliverable'.

Established by counting: pixel-core carries 252 `#[test]` functions across 29 source files. Of those, 33 are in terminal.rs, 12 in herdr.rs and 4 in ghostty.rs, so roughly 203 live in the modules the plan promises not to touch, and their fixtures are compiled-in fonts rather than system resources.

What follows: today those 203 tests cannot run on Windows at all, because lib.rs (lines 1–26) declares `mod terminal`, `mod herdr` and `pub mod ghostty` unconditionally, so the crate does not compile and nothing downstream of it is verifiable. The moment Task 2 lands the cfg gates, all 203 become a per-task regression net that runs on every subsequent task's 'tests must pass before Task N+1' gate. That converts the plan's central promise — nineteen modules unchanged — from an intention into something mechanically checked eleven times, and Task 12's `git diff` against the vendored baseline closes the loop on changes the tests would not catch.

This is also why Task 2's position before Tasks 3–7 is not arbitrary sequencing: every later task is being executed against a compiler and a test suite that work, rather than against a crate that cannot build. For autonomous execution that is the difference between a task that fails loudly and a task that produces plausible untested code.

What would overturn it: if a meaningful share of those 203 tests turn out to depend transitively on terminal.rs's `Terminal` struct rather than on its plain types, they would be cfg-gated off alongside it and the net would be thinner than the count suggests. I confirmed the coupling is mostly type-level (see the module-count finding) but did not compile the test tree to see how many survive gating.

findings.title: The brief undercounts its own evidence: the portable surface is 43 of 46 files, not 19 of 22
findings.body:
The '19 of 22 modules' row is the single piece of evidence the whole architectural bet rests on, so it is worth knowing that it is counted conservatively. Established: the 22 figure counts only top-level `.rs` files in `pixel-core/src`. There are five subdirectories — `engine/`, `scroll/`, `selection/`, `surfaces/`, `tree/` — holding 24 further `.rs` files, and `grep -rl` for rustix / std::os::unix / termios / libc:: / /dev/tty across all five returns nothing. So the accurate figure is 43 of 46 source files with zero unix references, and the compositor, layout, scroll, selection and tree machinery are all in the clean column.

What follows: the bet — keep pixel-core, replace its tty layer — is resting on a larger and more uniform base than the brief claims for it, which matters because you are weighing that bet against dropping pixel-core and rewriting the browser chrome.

One complication I should state in the same breath, because it bounds the claim: the `engine/` modules do reference `crate::terminal`, but for types rather than syscalls — `engine/doc.rs:6` imports `KeyEvent`, `engine/keys.rs:4` imports `KeyEvent`/`KeyKind`, `engine/input.rs:5` and `engine/embed.rs:5` import `Mouse`/`MouseKind`, and `engine/clipboard.rs:7` imports the `Terminal` struct itself. Those types are defined at terminal.rs:11–121 and are plain data. So the 43 files are portable but not fully decoupled: the seam Task 2 defines has to hand these types out, and `engine/clipboard.rs` is the one call site that wants the concrete `Terminal`. That is an argument that Task 2's instruction to 'derive the trait from terminal.rs's existing callers, not from a fresh design' is the correct instruction rather than boilerplate caution — the callers are enumerable and there are five of them.

What would overturn it: if `engine/clipboard.rs`'s use of the concrete `Terminal` reaches methods that are inherently fd-shaped rather than trait-able, that one module moves out of the free column. I read the import, not the body.
findings.fix: Correct the brief's table to 43 of 46 and add a row naming the five engine/ modules that import terminal.rs types, so Task 2's trait surface is derived from a written list rather than rediscovered.

findings.title: Task 7 is already upstream's default behaviour on Windows — the stock-Electron claim is not a plan, it is the existing code path
findings.body:
The brief argues stock Electron 'should work on Windows unmodified'. Reading the file, it is stronger than that: Windows already gets the right answer with no branch added.

Established from `offscreen.ts`: line 4 is `const SHM_FRAMES = process.platform === "linux" && process.env.TERMINAL_BROWSER_SHM !== "0"`, which is false on Windows. `offscreenPreferences` tests `process.platform === "darwin"` first, which is false, and falls to `{ useSharedTexture: false, useSharedMemory: SHM_FRAMES, deviceScaleFactor }` — i.e. `{useSharedTexture:false, useSharedMemory:false, deviceScaleFactor}`, which is exactly what Task 7's first bullet says to 'add a Windows branch' to return. `initOffscreenMode` throws only under `process.platform === "darwin" && !sharedTextures`, so on Windows it does not throw and logs mode `bitmap` — which is Task 7's second bullet, already satisfied.

Downstream is equally unguarded. `paint.ts:41–43`: `presentPaint` returns `presentTexture` if a texture is present, `presentShmFrame` if an shm frame is present, and otherwise `presentBitmap(surface, image, ...)` with no platform test at all. With both capabilities off, stock Electron's `paint` event supplies only the NativeImage, so `presentBitmap` — `image.toBitmap()` into `surface.present({bgra, width, height, damage})` — is what runs. And the seam is typed for it: `engine/packages/pixel-react/src/surface.ts:8` declares `{ bgra: Buffer; width: number; height: number } & Damaged` as a member of the frame union, routed at line 39 into `engine.updateSurface`.

What follows: Task 7 is not a porting task, it is a confirm-and-test task, and its cost estimate should drop accordingly. More usefully for your risk question, it means the Electron half of the bet needs no new code to be wrong in — the only genuinely new Windows code between Electron and the pane is the backend below `Surface.present`.

Two things I could not confirm, both in the same direction. First, `useSharedMemory` is not in Electron's public offscreen type — the return is cast `as Electron.WebPreferences["offscreen"]` — so it is an upstream-patch key; passing it as `false` to stock Electron should be inert, but I did not run Electron to verify it is ignored rather than rejected. Second, upstream has left a comment on the bgra union member at surface.ts:8 musing about removing that case, so the path the port depends on is one upstream has considered deleting; that bears on re-vendoring, not on whether it works today.
findings.fix: Rescope Task 7 from 'add a Windows branch' to 'assert the existing defaults resolve to bitmap on Windows and lock that in with the per-platform test' — an added branch would be dead code the tests then certify.

findings.title: Nothing else reaches this place: upstream's own tooling excludes Windows and the patched-Electron mirror has no Windows build
findings.body:
The case for acting includes what declining costs, and here declining does not mean 'wait for a better route' — I checked whether one exists.

Established: `scripts/install.sh:9–16` maps only `Darwin-arm64`, `Linux-x86_64|Linux-amd64` and `Linux-aarch64|Linux-arm64`, and everything else exits 1 with 'terminal-browser does not support …'. `scripts/fetch-electron.sh:9–11` offers the same three platforms and pulls from the `zenbu-labs/electron-releases` mirror at line 15. Independently confirmed by grep: there is no `cfg(…windows…)` anywhere in the engine workspace.

What follows: for upstream to reach Windows they would have to build and host a Windows Electron fork they do not currently produce, on top of porting the tty layer — i.e. strictly more work than this plan, which avoids the fork entirely by using the bitmap path. So there is no upstream-will-get-there-eventually option that arrives sooner or cheaper. With WSL ruled out by your framing, the alternative to this plan is not a slower browser in an agwinterm pane; it is no browser in an agwinterm pane.

What this unlocks that is otherwise out of reach is specific rather than general: agwinterm's graphics capability is currently exercised by one static-image producer. A Chromium surface in a pane makes the control-pipe image path a general rendering target, and the plan's own out-of-scope note identifies where that leads — stock Electron on Windows can expose a D3D11 shared-texture handle and agwinterm already renders with Direct2D, so a genuine zero-copy path exists behind this work and behind nothing else.

What would overturn it: upstream announcing or landing Windows support, which I could not check — this review has no network access, and the context directory contains no upstream issue tracker, release notes or roadmap. My evidence is the vendored tree at `.reference/terminal-browser/` as it stands, and it may be behind upstream's HEAD; `docs/design/UPSTREAM.md`, which would pin the commit, is only created at Task 1.

findings.title: pixel-node is already structured for a third platform, and the Owned path it hands Windows is tuned rather than vestigial
findings.body:
Task 6 reads like a porting task; the code suggests it is closer to filling in an existing pattern. Established: `pixel-node/Cargo.toml` puts rustix and libc under `[target.'cfg(target_os = "linux")'.dependencies]`, so the crate has no unconditional unix dependency; `lib.rs:5–12` gates `mod iosurface` on macos and `mod shm` on linux at the declaration, not inside the module. `surface.rs:7–17` defines `SurfacePixels` with `IoSurface` gated to macos, `Shm` gated to linux, and `Owned { bgra, width, height }` ungated — so on Windows the enum has exactly one variant, which is why the plan can say the Windows path 'already exists'.

The part worth knowing beyond that: `Owned` is not an unexercised fallback. `SurfaceMailbox::submit` at surface.rs:53–58 reclaims the dropped frame's `Vec<u8>` into `slot.spare` when a frame is coalesced, and the same buffer-reuse handling appears at lines 101, 125 and 146. Upstream built allocation recycling specifically around the owned-bitmap path. Combined with `BitmapPresenter`'s coalescing in `browser/src/page/paint.ts` — which unions damage rects across dropped frames — the copy path Windows inherits has already had its two obvious costs addressed by someone who cared about frame rate.

What would overturn it, and I want this stated rather than buried: I could not verify that pixel-node builds on Windows, because building is outside this review. Its dependency list includes `openh264 = { version = "0.9.7", features = ["source"] }`, which compiles C++ from source via a build script, plus seven tree-sitter grammars that also build C. Whether those compile under MSVC is unchecked and is a real Task 6 risk that the plan's checklist does not mention; my claim here is about the crate's own platform structure, not about its transitive build.
findings.fix: Add a bullet to Task 6 to build pixel-node's native dependencies (openh264 with the source feature, the tree-sitter grammars) under MSVC before touching draw_frame, so a toolchain problem surfaces as its own finding rather than as a confusing napi failure.

findings.title: The agwinterm half is chartered by agwinterm's own prior design and keeps its justification if winterm-browser stalls
findings.body:
On whether the two-repo split is right: the usual objection to splitting work across repos is that one half is dead weight without the other. That does not apply here, and the evidence predates this port.

Established from agwinterm's own documents: `docs/agterm-gap-analysis.md:41` marks 'Image protocols / graphics' as **Partial** and describes only the out-of-band file path; `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-06-30-agwinterm-design.md:204` records that animation and video-like Kitty frames are 'supported structurally but not the optimization target (docxy emits static images)'. So agwinterm named this exact gap for itself before winterm-browser existed. The dependency plan's own overview lists non-browser consumers — a video preview, an animating plot, a remote frame buffer — and locates the cost correctly ('the expensive part of image.frame is not the placement machinery, which is already good — it is the format and the transport'), which matches what I read in `HandleImageFrame`: the placement and caching machinery is sound and the PNG-file round trip is the only thing being replaced.

What follows: the split places the work in the repository whose own roadmap already wanted it, and the frameshm command is worth building on agwinterm's terms whether or not the browser port completes. That is a different and better reason for the split than 'these are two codebases'.

What would overturn it: if the frameshm layout ends up shaped narrowly around Electron's BGRA paint buffer, the general-purpose justification thins out. The plan's Task 1 header carries per-slot `(width, height, stride, format)` rather than a fixed format, which points the other way, but the spec does not exist yet — `docs/specs/image-frameshm.md` is a Task 1 deliverable and I confirmed it is not on disk today, which is also the thing Task 10's precondition is written to catch.
